Rejected offerings expose the honor people actually give

The book is built as a series of disputes. God makes a statement, and the people ask how (verses 2, 6, 7). Verse 8 gives a simple test. Would the governor accept a blind or lame animal as a gift? The priests give a human official more honor than God. Leviticus 22:20–22 required animals without defect. Verse 10 says closed doors would be better than such offerings.
Public teaching and private fidelity belong within the same dispute

Verse 13 shows worshipers weeping because their offerings are not accepted. They ask why. Verse 14 points away from the altar to the home. Each man has been faithless to the wife of his youth. She is called his companion and his wife by covenant. God stood as witness to that promise. The same word, “faithless,” describes the priests’ teaching in verses 10–11.
The desired visitor confronts the people who ask for justice

In 2:17 the people asked where the God of justice was. Verses 1–2 answer that he is coming. They then ask who can stand when he does. Those who called for justice are examined first. Verse 5 lists the charges. Sorcery, adultery, and false oaths stand beside unpaid wages. Wrongs to widows, orphans, and foreigners are named in the same breath.
The final warning joins remembered instruction with restored relationships

The book closes with two instructions. Verse 4 looks back: remember the law given through Moses. Verse 5 looks ahead: expect Elijah before the great day. Verse 6 says what Elijah will do. He will turn parents and children toward each other. The healing of families prepares for God’s coming. The other choice is named last, and it is a curse.
